segment_name: Opening: A Boy's Passage into Complexity

questions.question: Oliver, let's start with the very first sentence — 'Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life, or whether that station will be held by anybody else, these pages must show.' You've said that line is less about modesty and more like a performer stepping onstage and making a promise. Can you unpack that? What's Dickens actually doing there?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to open up his 'performance contract' thesis vividly and accessibly — sets up his core take early and invites the others to react

questions.question: Edmund, you've talked about this opening as Dickens doing something almost metaphysical — a person becoming aware they have a self to lose. But Oliver's just told us it's essentially theatrical. Are those two things compatible, or is one of them wrong?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to either defend the interior/metaphysical reading against Trevelyan's theatrical framing, or find interesting common ground — creates the first friction of the segment

questions.question: Daniel, I want to push on something. Edmund's saying David's vulnerability is really about his soul being tested — it's what reveals his capacity for goodness. You've said, if I've understood you right, that that reading is almost a kind of ideological sleight of hand — that calling it 'moral growth' obscures the fact that the boy is just being fed into a machine. Is that fair? And if so, what's the evidence in the opening pages?
questions.intent: Get Rosen to make his systemic/structural argument directly against Leigh's moral-growth reading — provoke the sharpest disagreement in the segment and push him toward specific textual evidence

questions.question: Edmund, Rosen's basically saying that when we talk about David 'choosing goodness despite circumstance,' we're letting the institutions off the hook — we're admiring the flower for blooming in the concrete instead of asking who poured the concrete. What's your answer to that?
questions.intent: Give Leigh the chance to defend the irreducible individual against Rosen's structural determinism — this is the segment's central intellectual fight and it should feel personal

questions.question: Oliver, you've said Dickens writes the voice before he writes the person — and your exhibit A is Peggotty. Can you actually do that for us? Read us a bit of Peggotty and show us what you mean — because I think that might cut right through this argument about whether Dickens is a social critic or a poet of the interior.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read aloud and demonstrate his thesis concretely — creates an audio moment, slightly wrong-foots the political debate, and lets Trevelyan's 'performance' argument land on its own terms rather than as theory

steering_notes: The central fault line is Rosen vs. Leigh — systemic critique versus moral individualism. Let that fight breathe, but don't let it become abstract. Push both of them back to specific moments in the text whenever the argument floats upward into theory. Trevelyan is the wild card: his theatrical/performative reading can either mediate between the two or blow the whole frame open, so use him strategically — open with him to set a vivid, accessible tone, then deploy him again near the end to shift the register if the Rosen-Leigh debate gets too locked. The goal is to end the segment with all three positions feeling genuinely alive and unresolved — don't let anyone 'win' the opening.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's claim that David's 'moral growth' is really socialization into accepting diminishment directly contradicts Leigh's claim that David *chooses* goodness — this is the segment's load-bearing disagreement and should be surfaced explicitly

Leigh's reading of the atmospheric details (the fens, Murdstone's severity) as 'the texture of a child's emotional world' runs straight into Rosen's reading of those same elements as the visible machinery of institutional power — worth asking both of them to look at the same passage

Trevelyan's insistence that Dickens 'demolishes' Victorian ideology rather than endorsing it is actually closer to Rosen than Trevelyan might admit — there's a productive moment where Rosen could claim Trevelyan as an unexpected ally, which would unsettle both of them

The opening narrator-in-retrospect frame is claimed by all three experts for very different purposes: Leigh sees metaphysical self-awareness, Rosen sees political retrospection, Trevelyan sees theatrical performance — worth naming this three-way split explicitly and letting them fight over a single sentence

segment_name: The Architecture of Shame: Class, Servitude, and Uriah Heep's Rise

questions.question: Oliver, you've said that Heep's villainy *is* his voice — that you have to hear him to understand him. Can you actually give us that? Read us the passage where he's doing that umble thing at full throttle, and tell us what you're hearing that a reader might miss on the page.
questions.intent: Get Oliver performing the passage aloud and making his case that the verbal texture is the whole architecture — sets up the table beautifully before the disagreement kicks in

questions.question: Daniel, Oliver just gave us Heep as a kind of grotesque entertainment, a voice to be savored. But you've been pretty sharp in your notes about the novel's own judgment of Heep being — and I'm quoting you here — 'convenient.' So what does Dickens actually show us about *why* Uriah became Uriah, and is the novel aware of what it's showing us?
questions.intent: Draw out Daniel's structural reading and his argument that the novel condemns Heep while inadvertently exposing the system that made him — gets the class critique fully on the table

questions.question: Edmund, I want to push you on something. Daniel's just argued that Heep's humility is a rational adaptation to a system that gave him no other ladder. You've said it's a moral choice, a corruption of the will. But when Heep himself explains his philosophy — and there's that extraordinary passage where he does — doesn't Dickens give him a kind of terrible *logic*? Is that the voice of a monster, or a man who's worked something out?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to reckon with the explanatory power of Heep's own speech and create direct confrontation with Daniel's reading — the 'choice vs. circumstance' argument made explicit

questions.question: Daniel, here's the thing I keep snagging on — David Copperfield himself is also an orphan, also without money, also has to perform respectability to get anywhere. Why does Dickens let David climb and destroy Uriah for climbing? Is David just a better liar, or is something else going on?
questions.intent: Provoke Daniel's sharpest take about how the system protects its own — also invites Oliver to push back on whether this reading makes David too knowing and Dickens too cynical

questions.question: Edmund, last one for you — and I want all three of you in on this. You've said Dickens's radicalism is moral, not political. Daniel thinks it's structural. Oliver thinks it might just be theatrical. Can a character be all three at once, or does picking one of those readings mean you're getting Dickens wrong?
questions.intent: Force a three-way synthesis or final disagreement — gives each expert a chance to either defend their lane or make a surprising concession, strong close to the segment

steering_notes: The productive fault line here is Oliver vs. Daniel vs. Edmund on what Heep *is* — a voice, a symptom, or a soul. Don't let them talk past each other; when Edmund says 'moral choice' and Daniel says 'structural product,' make them fight over the same passage. The David Copperfield comparison question (Q4) is the wildcard most likely to produce something none of them has fully thought through — sit with the silence after it. Keep Oliver honest: he'll want to retreat into close reading when the politics get hot, but his point about performance is actually the most interesting bridge between Daniel and Edmund if you can push him there.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's 'we're meant to enjoy the villainy' directly undercuts Daniel's claim that the novel's judgment is an ideological convenience — Oliver is saying the judgment is aesthetic, not moral, which is a third option neither Daniel nor Edmund has accounted for

Edmund's insistence on 'moral choice' is the sharpest direct contradiction of Daniel's 'rational adaptation' reading — make them share the same passage and interpret it against each other in real time
Daniel's reading of David as a fellow climber who escapes punishment will irritate Edmund, who sees David's rise as morally earned — this is the argument most likely to generate heat

Oliver's claim that Dickens gives us behavior not introspection sits in interesting tension with Edmund's psychological reading — if Dickens only shows us the surface, how does Edmund know what's happening in Heep's soul?

segment_name: Steerforth's Charisma and the Corruption of Friendship

questions.question: Oliver, you described Steerforth as an 'artist manqué' — a performer with no worthy stage. But I want to push you on that, because it sounds almost like an excuse. Dickens gives us this man who ruins Emily, who uses David, who treats people like props in his own drama — and you're saying the tragedy is that his *talent* went to waste? Isn't that a bit like feeling sorry for a con artist because he could have been a great novelist?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to defend and sharpen his 'artist manqué' thesis — and flag its tension with moral accountability — before Edmund inevitably pounces

questions.question: Edmund, you said David's failure is a moral one — that he *chooses* not to see what Steerforth is. But when you read the reunion passage, the one where David describes Steerforth with that almost worshipful language — does it actually read like a man making a choice? Or does Dickens write it so that the reader falls for it too? Because if we fall for it, can we really call it David's moral negligence?
questions.intent: Force Edmund to address the reader's own complicity — his strongest take — while provoking Oliver and Daniel to weigh in on whether 'choice' is the right frame

questions.question: Daniel, you made a point that stopped me cold in our chat — you said Steerforth isn't a wasted talent, he's actually a *success*. He gets what he wants, he moves through the world with impunity. So if that's right, what exactly is Dickens asking us to mourn at the end? Because the drowning feels like it's meant to hit us hard — is that just Dickens having it both ways?
questions.intent: Get Daniel to articulate the structural critique at its sharpest — that the novel's emotional register may be in tension with its social diagnosis — and invite Oliver to respond on the question of genuine tragic loss

questions.question: Daniel, you said the seduction of Emily and the seduction of David are basically the same mechanism — charm as a predatory tool. Oliver, I know you'll have something to say about this. But Daniel, if that's true, why does Dickens keep making Steerforth so *magnetic* on the page? Is Dickens exposing the system, or is he in some sense reproducing it — letting us enjoy the charisma even as he's supposedly condemning it?
questions.intent: Trigger the core disagreement between Daniel's structural reading and Oliver's aesthetic one — is Dickens complicit in Steerforth's seduction? Draw out Edmund too on whether the reader's pleasure is part of the moral test

questions.question: Oliver, you said the older David narrating is still under the spell — that decades later he hasn't fully broken free. Edmund thinks that's David's moral failure. Daniel thinks it's evidence that David never really understood the class dynamics at work. But you're suggesting something different — that the spell persists because David *recognises something of himself* in Steerforth. Can you find us the moment in the text where you feel that most — where David's admiration tips into something more uncomfortable than simple hero-worship?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to quote a specific passage and articulate the psychological mirror thesis — David and Steerforth as doubles — which neither Edmund nor Daniel has fully engaged with, and which should generate strong cross-talk

steering_notes: The richest tension in this segment is the three-way split on what kind of tragedy Steerforth represents: Oliver sees aesthetic waste, Edmund sees moral failure, Daniel sees systemic production. Don't let any one frame dominate too early — use the first two questions to establish the positions, then use questions 3-5 to force them into direct collision. The reader-complicity angle (do we enjoy Steerforth too much?) is the liveliest common ground and should surface by the midpoint. Keep pushing for specific passages — all three experts have strong textual instincts and the conversation will get abstract without anchoring. If Edmund starts moralising in the abstract, redirect to the reunion passage. If Daniel goes too structural, pull him back to Emily-versus-David as a concrete comparison. Watch Oliver — he has the most contrarian take and may need space to develop it before the others talk over him.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's 'artist manqué' thesis directly challenges Daniel's claim that Steerforth is a 'success' — for Oliver there is genuine tragic waste, for Daniel that framing romanticises what is actually a story of impunity; this is the sharpest direct collision and should be engineered explicitly

Edmund's insistence that David *chooses* not to see is in direct tension with Daniel's argument that David never fully understands his own vulnerability — one implies moral agency, the other implies structural blindness; ask them to address each other directly on this

Oliver's claim that David recognises himself in Steerforth (the hunger for effect) is unexplored by both Edmund and Daniel — it reframes the friendship as a mirror relationship rather than a seduction, and both will want to push back from their respective positions

Daniel's parallel between the seduction of Emily and the seduction of David should be put to Oliver, who may resist collapsing the distinction between aesthetic admiration and predatory exploitation — this could be the most heated exchange of the segment

segment_name: Dickens at Play: Comic Eccentricity and Moral Insight

questions.question: Oliver, you've said we're basically reading Dickens wrong if we're reading him silently. So let's test that — can you actually give us Micawber right now? One of those speeches where he's winding himself up into full rhetorical flight while everything around him is falling apart. And then tell us what we'd miss if we just read it on the page.
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform a Micawber passage aloud, demonstrating his 'writing for the actor's mouth' thesis and setting up the core debate about whether the comedy is aesthetic, moral, or diagnostic

questions.question: Daniel, you just heard that — and I know you have a different account of why Micawber speaks that way. Oliver's hearing virtuoso English; you're hearing something else. What are you hearing?
questions.intent: Provoke direct disagreement between Rosen and Trevelyan — Rosen should articulate that Micawber's verbal inflation isn't just beautiful language but mirrors financial speculation and class desperation, pushing back on Trevelyan's aesthetic reading

questions.question: Edmund, I want to bring you in here because you've said something that cuts against both of them — that Dickens's comedy isn't really satire or diagnosis, it's closer to what Johnson meant by moral instruction. But here's what I'm wrestling with: when we laugh at Micawber, are we laughing *at* a man destroyed by debt, or are we laughing *with* something more universal? Where does the charity come in?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's humanist reading and create a three-way tension — Leigh argues for universal moral recognition, Rosen wants structural critique, Trevelyan wants sonic performance; force Leigh to locate exactly where sympathy and comedy meet

questions.question: Daniel, Edmund just used the word 'universal' — and I have a feeling that's exactly the word you'd want to interrogate. Is calling these characters universal a way of letting Dickens, and us, off the hook?
questions.intent: Provoke the sharpest version of Rosen's critique — that universalising the eccentrics dissolves the specific Victorian economic conditions that produced them, and that sentiment becomes a substitute for structural thinking

questions.question: Oliver, last word to you on this — both Daniel and Edmund are making Dickens's comedy do serious argumentative work, one for economics, one for moral philosophy. But you've suggested the comedy might be doing something that precedes all of that: that the English language itself is somehow inherently comic, and Micawber and Mrs. Gummidge and Uriah Heep are basically proof of that. Is that a claim you'd actually defend? Because it sounds almost too large.
questions.intent: Give Trevelyan space to make his boldest, most sweeping claim about Dickens and the comic nature of English speech itself — designed to be a provocation that Rosen and Leigh will both want to respond to, and a strong closing note for the segment

steering_notes: The productive tension here is a three-way: Trevelyan wants performance and sound, Rosen wants economic structure, Leigh wants moral universals. Don't let it become a two-way fight between Rosen and Leigh while Trevelyan does impressions — keep pulling Trevelyan's performative claims back into contact with the interpretive stakes. The best radio moment will be if Rosen directly challenges whether Leigh's 'we laugh in recognition of ourselves' is a politically comfortable move. Let that breathe. Also: if Trevelyan actually performs Micawber well, the segment will have an energy spike early — ride that, don't cut it off for a question.
cross_engagement_targets: Rosen's claim that Micawber's verbal inflation 'mirrors financial speculation itself' directly contradicts Trevelyan's reading of the same speeches as linguistic vitality and virtuoso performance — same passage, opposite diagnosis; push them to name what they're actually disagreeing about

Leigh's insistence that comedy functions as 'illumination' rather than 'irony or critique' is a direct rebuttal to Rosen's framework before Rosen has even made it — flag this to Leigh and ask if he's anticipating a reading he finds reductive

Trevelyan and Leigh are closer than they realise — both resist treating the eccentrics as social symptoms — but their reasons differ fundamentally (Trevelyan: sonic performance; Leigh: moral instruction). A question that forces them to articulate that difference could be more generative than the Rosen-Leigh clash

segment_name: The Fog Lifts: Atmosphere, Setting, and the Bildungsroman's Dark Spaces

questions.question: Oliver, you've said the fog and darkness in this novel aren't really symbolism — they're staging. That's a pretty provocative claim. Can you take us to a specific passage, one of those warehouse scenes, and actually show us what you mean? Like, what are you *hearing* when you read it that the rest of us might be missing?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read aloud and demonstrate his 'sound design' thesis with a specific passage — opens the segment with a concrete, sensory hook and establishes the performative-vs-symbolic debate early

questions.question: Daniel, I want to push on something. You're saying the bildungsroman form is basically ideological machinery — that it converts David's radical child-eye view of injustice into adult acceptance. But Oliver just made the case that this is all theatre, performance, Dickens the entertainer. Is that a dodge? Is calling it 'genius stagecraft' just another way of not dealing with what the fog is actually hiding?
questions.intent: Set up the central disagreement between Oliver's performative reading and Daniel's structural critique — force Daniel to either engage with or dismiss the entertainment argument directly

questions.question: Edmund, you've been patient — I can see you wanting to jump in. Because if I'm reading you right, you think both of them are missing the point. Daniel wants the fog to be capitalism, Oliver wants it to be theatre — and you want it to be something more like a moral gymnasium. David walks through the dark and we find out what he's made of. Is that fair? And is that a harder sell than it used to be?
questions.intent: Draw out Edmund's individual moral drama thesis and put it in direct contrast with Daniel's structural reading — also probe whether Edmund acknowledges any tension in defending a character-forging-in-hardship argument in 2024

questions.question: Daniel, Edmund just said — and I think he means this seriously — that the darkness is the *occasion* for testing character, not a critique of the system that produced it. You've called that kind of reading almost a kind of moral consolation prize. So I'll put it to you directly: is Edmund wrong, or is he describing something real that just doesn't go far enough?
questions.intent: Force a direct engagement between Edmund and Daniel on the moral-drama-vs-structural-critique fault line — avoid letting Daniel simply dismiss Edmund; push for a more nuanced collision

questions.question: Last one, and I want to bring it back to the reading experience, because Oliver I suspect you have a view on this. Daniel's talking about the fog closing back in on David once he's comfortable and propertied. Edmund's talking about David emerging good from the darkness. But you've said Peggotty's domestic scenes are where warmth actually *enters* the novel — through voice, through dialogue, not description. Is that Dickens offering us an alternative to both those readings? A place where the darkness just... doesn't get to be the point?
questions.intent: Use the Peggotty counterpoint to create a moment of unexpected convergence or productive complication — does domestic warmth undercut both the ideological and the moral-drama readings? Let all three respond

steering_notes: The segment has a natural arc: open with Oliver making the performative case concrete and sensory, then let Daniel's structural challenge hit it, then bring Edmund in as the third term who reframes the whole debate around moral character. The real productive tension is Edmund vs Daniel — Oliver's 'it's theatre' position can actually float above both and keep returning to defuse standoffs with a reminder that the text itself is doing something to us as readers, whatever we think it means. Watch for Daniel going too abstract-theoretical; bring him back to specific passages when that happens. Edmund may sound conservative — don't let him be dismissed too quickly, that reading has genuine textual support and makes for better radio if it's taken seriously. Try to end on the Peggotty question, which is deliberately warmer and more ambiguous — gives the segment somewhere to breathe after the ideological sparring.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver's claim that the prose *tempo* of the warehouse scenes is 'sound design not symbolism' directly challenges Daniel's reading of those same scenes as evidence of material deprivation — they're looking at the same passages and hearing completely different things. Get them to actually compare notes on one passage.

Edmund's argument that the fog tests individual character ('will David steal? will he despair?') is almost a direct answer to Daniel's claim that David learns complicity rather than virtue — they are offering opposite moral verdicts on the same developmental arc. This is the sharpest disagreement in the segment and should be surfaced explicitly.

Daniel's point that 'the fog doesn't lift for Uriah Heep' is a genuine textual observation that neither Oliver nor Edmund addresses in pre-interview — worth directing at both of them as a challenge to their respective readings.

segment_name: Social Machinery and Individual Will: Dickens's Persistent Critique

questions.question: Edmund, you've said Dickens is fundamentally a novelist of conscience — that the fog and the grinding institutions are really just backdrop for the soul's journey. But Daniel would say that's exactly the ideological sleight of hand the novel performs on its readers. So let me put it directly: when Uriah Heep is 'umble, is that a moral failing, or is Dickens showing us a man who had no other move available to him?
questions.intent: Get Edmund to commit to the moral-character reading, which sets up Daniel's structural counter and Oliver's voice-and-performance angle — the three positions collide fastest if Edmund goes first and goes hard

questions.question: Daniel, you want to quote the moments where David's narration becomes most unreliable — where he congratulates himself on rising without mentioning Betsey's money or Copperfield's name. Can you find us one of those passages and just read it? Because I want the others to hear what you're hearing when you call this Dickens's most insidious move.
questions.intent: Get a specific passage read aloud, let the text do the argumentative work, and force Oliver and Edmund to respond to the actual words rather than a paraphrase of Daniel's thesis

questions.question: Oliver, you've argued we literally have to hear this novel to understand it — that Uriah Heep's repetition of 'umble' turns the character into a kind of machine of insincerity and you only feel that when it's performed. So perform it. Give us a bit of Uriah. And then tell us: is what we just heard a man, or is it a system wearing a man's face?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read aloud and make the case through performance rather than argument — creates a genuinely different radio moment, and the 'man or system' framing directly provokes both Daniel and Edmund

questions.question: Daniel, Oliver thinks Dickens is an optimist about individual will — that the redemption arcs are *earned*, not sentimental. You've said suffering in this novel teaches you nothing except how to perform the role already assigned to you. Those are completely opposite readings of the same book. Who actually gets redeemed in David Copperfield, and what did they already have going in?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Daniel's structural pessimism and Oliver's redemptive reading — the question 'who gets redeemed and what did they start with' is concrete enough to produce real disagreement rather than talking past each other

questions.question: Edmund, last one for you — and I want you to be honest about this. You've said Dickens's salvation is personal virtue: Peggotty's faithfulness, Agnes's constancy. But Daniel would say those virtues are distributed very precisely along class lines in this novel. Agnes gets to be constant because she's comfortable. Peggotty gets to be faithful in service. Does Dickens give the poor a path to virtue that doesn't require them to stay in their lane?
questions.intent: Push Edmund to the hardest version of his own argument — if individual moral character is the answer, why does the novel's distribution of virtue track so neatly onto social position? This is the sharpest cross-engagement point between Edmund and Daniel

steering_notes: The three positions here are genuinely irreconcilable in the best way — Edmund wants moral conscience, Daniel wants structural critique, Oliver wants performed voice as the site of meaning. Don't let them find a false synthesis too early. The productive tension is: can all three be right simultaneously, or does the novel ultimately tip one way? Push toward concrete passages whenever the conversation goes abstract — the text is the best referee. Watch for Oliver trying to mediate between Edmund and Daniel through the 'both/and' of performance; let him make that move but make Daniel challenge whether aesthetic complexity lets Dickens off the structural hook.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel's claim that David's narration is ideologically self-serving directly contradicts Oliver's claim that Dickens animates individuals through language in ways that expose the machinery — Oliver hears critique in the prose music; Daniel hears self-justification; this is the sharpest disagreement and needs a dedicated moment

Edmund's reading of Uriah Heep as a study in wounded pride and false humility versus Daniel's reading of Uriah as the man the system produced from the same raw material as David — same character, opposite diagnoses, force them to the text together

Oliver's insistence on reading aloud as interpretive method is itself a methodological challenge to Daniel's sociological reading — at some point ask Daniel whether the performance dimension changes his analysis or whether it's just aestheticizing ideology

segment_name: Closing: The Heart Disciplined, The Story Redeemed

questions.question: Edmund, you said something in our chat that stuck with me — that Agnes isn't a reward, she's a test. Can you unpack that? Because I think most people hear 'Agnes' and think 'boring Victorian angel-wife.' What are we missing?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's strongest take on Agnes as disciplined love rather than sentimental prize, and set up the others to react to the moral framework he's building

questions.question: Daniel, I want to put something to you directly — Edmund just described David's ending as ruthlessly unsentimental, earned through surrendering illusions. But you've basically said the whole 'earning it' narrative is rigged from the start. So who's right? Is this a story of genuine moral growth, or is it a story about what moral growth looks like when you already have all the advantages?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Leigh's moral-interior reading and Rosen's structural critique — get them talking to each other rather than past each other

questions.question: Oliver, you've argued that the ending's quietness is actually Dickens at his most sophisticated — that *not* performing is itself a performance. But Daniel would say that quietness is doing ideological work, smoothing over all the wreckage. And Edmund would say it's moral seriousness. How do you hear it? When David finally settles into that calm, do you feel earned restraint, or do you hear something being suppressed?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to defend the literary-aesthetic case for the ending while engaging with both the moral and political challenges the others have raised — ideally quote a passage of quiet prose

questions.question: Daniel, let's get specific — there's that moment near the end where David reflects back on his younger self and his undisciplined heart almost with tenderness. Oliver hears generosity in that voice, Edmund hears hard-won humility. You've said you'd read it as self-congratulation that reveals how thoroughly he's absorbed the system's logic. Can you actually read us that passage and show us what you mean? What's the tell?
questions.intent: Force a close-reading moment from Rosen using a specific passage — make the ideological critique textual rather than abstract, and let the others respond to the actual words

questions.question: Last one — and I want all three of you on this. Oliver, you said the real victory is that Dickens proves you can write a novel of theatrical delight *and* genuine human growth in the same breath. But by the end, Micawber's in Australia, Uriah's in prison, Emily's exiled, Steerforth's dead. The comic world has been — what's your word — metabolized. Does David's mature voice actually contain all of that, or does it just eulogize it from a safe distance?
questions.intent: Bring the conversation to a close by testing Trevelyan's 'metabolized multitudes' thesis against the actual fates of the novel's most vivid characters — designed to draw all three experts into a final exchange about what the ending costs

steering_notes: This segment has real combustion potential between Leigh and Rosen — one is arguing for the primacy of individual moral conscience, the other is arguing that individual moral conscience is a class-inflected luxury. Don't let Trevelyan become a referee; push him to take sides aesthetically and make the others engage with his literary claims. The goal is to end on a genuinely unresolved question: does the novel's emotional authority vindicate its redemptive frame, or does it inadvertently expose it? Let that tension sit rather than resolving it neatly. Keep Rosen from going too academic — push him back to the text whenever he abstracts. Keep Leigh from sounding preachy — the 'death of fancy, birth of genuine regard' framing is gold if he delivers it personally rather than programmatically.
cross_engagement_targets: Leigh's claim that Agnes represents 'disciplined love rather than sentimental prize' directly contradicts Rosen's implication that the Agnes ending is wish-fulfillment for a protagonist who has absorbed class ideology — this is the sharpest point of friction and should be surfaced early

Trevelyan's 'metabolized multitudes' thesis (the grotesques live on in David's voice) is in direct tension with Rosen's observation that those characters are materially destroyed and exiled — Trevelyan needs to answer whether literary absorption is an adequate response to narrative abandonment

Leigh and Rosen have a deeper structural disagreement: Leigh locates redemption in individual conscience in the Burkean tradition, Rosen locates the novel's real meaning in what it shows systemically despite itself — this is a genuine political-philosophical clash that can anchor the whole segment if surfaced explicitly
